Frailty means the state or quality of being weak, delicate, and easily damaged or broken. Think of something fragile — a thin piece of glass, a dried leaf, an old photograph — and frailty is the name for that condition of fragility. It describes something or someone that lacks the strength or toughness to resist harm, pressure, or the passage of time.

Frailty works in two closely related but distinct ways:

1. Physical frailty refers to bodily weakness — a lack of physical strength, robustness, or health. When someone is physically frail, their body is delicate and easily harmed. This is why the word is most commonly associated with old age and serious illness. An elderly person whose bones are brittle, whose muscles have weakened, and whose immune system can barely fight off a cold — that person is experiencing frailty. The word captures not just weakness, but vulnerability: the sense that very little force is needed to cause damage.

You could also use it for things, not just people. The frailty of an old bridge means it could collapse under pressure that a stronger bridge would handle easily.

2. Moral frailty (also called human frailty) refers to weakness of character — a person's tendency to make poor choices, give in to temptation, or fail to live up to their own values or ideals. This is not about physical strength at all; it is about the inner person. Every human being, no matter how good or wise, has moments of selfishness, dishonesty, or weakness of will. Those failings are our frailties. This sense of the word has been used for centuries to describe the imperfect, fallible nature of human beings in general.
An Important Nuance: Sympathy, Not Harshness

Notice that "frailty" almost always carries a gentle, sympathetic tone — especially in the moral sense. When someone acknowledges "human frailty," they are not condemning people; they are recognizing that being weak sometimes is part of being human. It is an honest, humble acknowledgment of limitation, not a cruel criticism. This is what separates "frailty" from a word like "corruption" or "wickedness," which imply deliberate wrongdoing. Frailty suggests a kind of helplessness or inevitability to the weakness.

When you use the plural form frailties, you are referring to specific, individual weaknesses — not the general condition, but the particular ways in which someone falls short. For example: "We must learn to accept each other's frailties." Here, the word points to concrete, nameable flaws — perhaps one person is easily angered, another is prone to dishonesty under pressure, another cannot resist a bad habit. Each of these is a frailty. Together, they are someone's frailties.
How Frailty Differs from Similar Words

Weakness is the closest word to frailty, but frailty is stronger and more specific. Weakness is a general, everyday word. Frailty implies a deeper, more fragile, more fundamental kind of weakness — one that is harder to overcome and that leaves someone especially exposed to damage or failure.

Fragility overlaps strongly with the physical sense of frailty, but fragility is used more for objects and things. Frailty is used more for living beings — people, bodies, characters — and carries more emotional weight.

Infirmity is similar to physical frailty but leans more toward specific medical conditions and disabilities, whereas frailty describes the overall state of being weak and vulnerable.

Here are examples that show you how naturally the word appears:

  • "The doctors were concerned about the patient's increasing frailty after the surgery."
  • "She helped her grandfather up the steps, aware of his frailty."
  • "The novel explores human frailty — how even the most principled people can fail when tested."
  • "He confessed his frailties openly, asking for forgiveness."
  • "The frailty of the old rope meant it could snap at any moment."
  • "Political power can expose the frailties of even the most admired leaders."

If you had to hold one idea in your mind about this word, let it be this: frailty is the condition of being easily broken — in body or in character. It is a word that looks honestly at limitation, whether that is an aging body losing its strength or a human soul losing its resolve. It is neither a cruel word nor a soft one — it is simply an honest one, and that is what gives it its quiet power.
